title: A Cat in a Hat
bodyHtml:
Chintang (Chintang: छिन्ताङ् Chintāṅ / Chhintang) is an eastern Kiranti language spoken by 5,000 to 6,000 people in Chhintang and Ahale municipalities of Dhankuta District, Koshi Zone, Nepal. Its dialects are Mulgaun and Sambhugaon. A few of the characters used to represent the words in this language may be unfamiliar. ʔ is a glottal stop, the sound heard in the middle of “uh-oh.” ŋ is the sound made by the ng in sing. ʌ is the sound made by the o in won.

Below are 16 sentences in Chintang written in the International Phonetic Alphabet, and their unordered English translations:

1.cuwa uthurumbeʔ yuŋnoa.There is a hole in the towel.
2.appa chintaŋbeʔ yuŋnob.The woman has gone away.
3.sencak siec.The rice has been cooked.
4.wapaŋa topi wadaŋsed.There is a hat on the head.
5.kok thuktaŋsee.My mother-in-law slept.
6.ram harinɨŋ khoŋnof.You go to the market.
7.kʌp kedadaŋseg.The water is in his mouth.
8.taŋbeʔ topi yuŋnoh.Joge sent a letter.
9.menwaŋa sencak sedei.The mouse died.
10.tawelbeʔ uhoŋ yuŋnoj.The woman has bought a chicken.
11.anambaŋa cuwa thuŋnok.The cup has been broken.
12.mechacha khadaŋsel.My father is in Chintang.
13.jogeŋa citthi haktem.The rooster has put on a hat.
14.anamma imsen.A cat killed a mouse.
15.hana bajar akhaʔnoo.Ram plays with Hari.
16.mechachaŋa wa khedoŋsep.My father-in-law drinks water.

B1. Match the Chintang sentences (1-16) with their corresponding English translation (a-p).

B2. Translate the following into Chintang. Note that some English words may be translated as part of a Chintang word.

  1. There is a cat in a hat.
  2. Joge plays with a chicken.
  3. My hen is in the market.
  4. parent-in-law

B3. Translate the following into English. Your answers should be structurally similar to the English translations given in the data.

  1. athurumbeʔ kok yuŋno
  2. appa khade
  3. anamma ammanɨŋ yuŋno

hints.text: Start with the endings that repeat across many sentences: -beʔ, -ŋa, -nɨŋ, and the verb endings -no, -e, -se. Then look for the names (Ram, Hari, Joge) and for the English sentences that contain a place, a location, or two people, since those give you the fastest secure matches.

Chintang puts the verb at the end of the sentence, and grammatical information is glued onto words as prefixes and suffixes rather than written as separate words. So an English phrase like "in the ..." or "with ..." or "my ..." corresponds to a piece attached to a Chintang noun, not to a word of its own. Sort the sentences by which of these attached pieces they contain, and sort the English list by whether it says "in/on", "with", or "my".

Try one piece of morphology out on the kinship words. Two words in the data begin with the same three letters anam- and differ only in their final syllable, -ma versus -ba. Two of the English sentences talk about in-laws, one female and one male, so those endings must be marking female versus male. Once you believe that, check whether the same -ma and -ba endings show up on any animal word, and what is left over when you peel them off.

explanationHtml:
What kind of language is this?

Chintang builds words by gluing pieces (called affixes) onto roots: a prefix goes in front, a suffix behind. English uses separate little words like in, with and my; Chintang attaches them. Also, the verb comes last in the sentence. Knowing just that, you can start matching.

Step 1: find the repeated suffix -beʔ

Look at the sentences containing -beʔ: uthurumbeʔ, chintaŋbeʔ, taŋbeʔ, tawelbeʔ. On the English side exactly four sentences say in or on a place: in the towel, in Chintang, in his mouth, on the head. So -beʔ is a location marker meaning "in / on / at".

chintaŋbeʔ obviously contains the place name Chintang, and tawelbeʔ contains a borrowed word for towel. That pins two matches immediately. All four of these sentences end in yuŋno, and all four English versions say something "is" somewhere, so yuŋno means "is located / there is".

Step 2: find the doer marker -ŋa

Four sentences have a word ending in -ŋa: wapaŋa, menwaŋa, anambaŋa, jogeŋa, mechachaŋa. Each of those sentences has two participants (someone does something to something). English sentences with two participants: a cat killed a mouse, the rooster put on a hat, the woman bought a chicken, Joge sent a letter, my father-in-law drinks water. jogeŋa gives away the Joge sentence. The suffix -ŋa marks the doer (linguists call this an ergative marker).

Compare sencak sie (one participant) with menwaŋa sencak sede (two participants): the same noun sencak appears in both, and the verb root se-/si- shows up in both. On the English side, "the mouse died" and "a cat killed a mouse" share the same participant too. So sencak is "mouse" and menwa is "cat".

Step 3: the suffix -nɨŋ

harinɨŋ contains the name Hari plus -nɨŋ, and the only English sentence with "with" is the one about Ram and Hari. So -nɨŋ means "with" and khoŋno means "plays".

Step 4: kinship words and the prefix a-

Notice appa, amma (in B3), anamma, anamba, awama. They all start with a-, and every English gloss for them says "my". So a- is "my". Compare cuwa uthurumbeʔ yuŋno = "The water is in his mouth" with B3's athurumbeʔ: the same root thurum "mouth" takes u- for "his" and a- for "my".

Now strip a- off the in-law words: nam-ma and nam-ba. The root nam means "parent-in-law", and -ma is female while -ba is male. That answers B2d.

The very same female/male suffixes appear on the animal word wa "chicken": wapa (the sentence about a rooster) is the male bird, so wa-ma with "my" in front, awama, is "my hen" - that is what B2c needs.

Step 5: the verb endings

Three tense patterns show up:

  • -no: present / general statement - yuŋno "is", thuŋno "drinks", khoŋno "plays", akhaʔno "you go".
  • -e: simple past - sie "died", sede "killed", hakte "sent", imse "slept", khade "went".
  • -aŋse / -oŋse: perfect, "has ..." - thuktaŋse "has been cooked", khadaŋse "has gone away", khedoŋse "has bought", wadaŋse "has put on", kedadaŋse "has been broken".

That is why appa khade in B3 is a simple past "went away", not "has gone away": the perfect version would be khadaŋse, which is the sentence about the woman.

Step 6: leftovers

Borrowed words help mop up the rest: topi "hat", kʌp "cup", citthi "letter", bajar "market", tawel "towel". hana is "you" (and the verb carries an extra a- for a second-person subject), kok is "rice", cuwa is "water", uhoŋ is "hole", taŋ is "head", mechacha is "woman".

Step 7: building the B2 sentences

For "There is a cat in a hat": the location word takes -beʔ, the thing located comes next, and the existential verb goes last, exactly as in the four -beʔ ... yuŋno models. For "Joge plays with a chicken": copy the Ram-and-Hari pattern, with -nɨŋ attached to the animal word. For "My hen is in the market": a- plus the female animal word, then the market word plus -beʔ, then the verb.
_reviewNotes: All answer keys are copied from the official solution page (B1 1-16, B2 a-d, B3 a-c). Points distributed as B1 0.5 each (8 total), B2 1 each (4), B3 1 each (3) = 15; the official booklet shows no per-part breakdown, so this split is editorial. Special characters to verify in the data: glottal stop ʔ, velar nasal ŋ, ʌ (in kʌp), barred i ɨ (in harinɨŋ, wanɨŋ, ammanɨŋ), and the Devanagari छिन्ताङ् plus Chintāṅ in the first paragraph - a font subset covering Devanagari and IPA is needed. Note sentence 7 is printed as 'kʌp kedadaŋse' in the booklet (three syllables 'keda-daŋse'); please confirm against the PDF. B1 choices are bare letters a-p to match the letter-only answer key.
